meaning: Asks how someone feels about something, how things are going, or what they think. It is also used to offer or suggest something.
connection: Noun + は + どうですか／いかがですか

senses.label: Asking for impressions
senses.meaning: Asks how the listener feels about something, or how it's going: “How is ...?” For past experiences, use 「どうでしたか」.
senses.connection: Noun + はどうですか／はどうでしたか (often with 仕事, 生活, 味, 天気, etc.)
examples: How is life in Japan?
How was yesterday's test?
How does it taste?

senses.label: Offering something
senses.meaning: Offers food, drinks or things: “Would you like ...?” Use the more polite 「いかがですか」 with guests and older people.
senses.connection: Noun + はいかがですか／はどうですか (often with お茶, コーヒー, お菓子, etc.)
examples: Would you like some coffee?
How about some of this cake, too?

senses.label: Suggesting a time or plan
senses.meaning: Suggests a time, place or plan and asks if it works: “How about ...?” 「いかがでしょうか」 is the very polite version.
senses.connection: Time / place noun + はどうですか／はいかがでしょうか
examples: How about tomorrow afternoon?
Would next Monday work for you?

notes: With bosses, clients and guests, 「〜はどう？」 or 「〜はどうですか」 sounds too casual. Use 「いかがですか」 to offer things and 「いかがでしょうか」 to suggest a time or plan: ✕「部長、明日はどう？」→ ○「部長、明日はいかがでしょうか」.
For something that has already happened, use the past tense: ✕「昨日の旅行はどうですか」→ ○「昨日の旅行はどうでしたか」.

When offered something, a bare 「いいです」 or 「けっこうです」 can leave the other person unsure whether you mean “yes, please” or “no, thanks”. To decline, start with 「いいえ」 and add 「もう十分です」 or 「大丈夫です」; to accept, say 「いただきます」.
Advice about what someone should do uses 「〜たらどうですか」, but it can sound preachy or even reproachful, and it is rude toward superiors: ✕「部長、休んだらどうですか」→ ○「少しお休みになってはいかがですか」.

daily.description: Your friend just started a new job, and you ask how it's going.
daily.example: How's the new job?

daily.description: The host serves tea and snacks to a visiting friend.
daily.example: Would you like some tea?

daily.title: Making plans with a friend
daily.description: Deciding on a day to meet up.
daily.example: How about Saturday?

work.example: Would ten o'clock next Wednesday work for you?

work.title: A waiter's suggestion
work.description: A waiter offers something to a customer.
work.example: Would you like dessert after your meal?

etymology: 「どう」 is a question word asking about manner or state: “how”. 「いかが」 is thought to come from old 「いかにか」 (如何にか) through sound changes. It is more refined and polite than 「どう」. It can be written 「如何」, but kana is normal.
formation: It is made of three parts: noun + 「は」, 「どう」 and 「ですか」. 「は」 first puts something forward as the topic, 「どう」 is a question adverb asking “in what state or manner”, and 「ですか」 makes the sentence a polite question. Put forward something the listener has already experienced and ask “how is it?”, and you are asking for impressions; put forward something they don't have yet, or a time not yet decided, and you are in effect offering or suggesting it. 「いかが」 is a more refined synonym of 「どう」, so switching to 「いかがですか」 gives the polite version used with guests and in business.

similar.title: 〜たらどうですか
similar.explanation: 「〜たらどうですか」 follows the た-form of a verb and suggests what the listener should do (“Why don't you ...?”), often with a lecturing tone. 「〜はどうですか」 follows a noun and asks for impressions or offers something. Both contain 「どう」, but the latter is more neutral.

similar.title: 〜ませんか
similar.explanation: 「〜ませんか」 uses a verb to invite someone to do something together: 「一緒に行きませんか」. 「〜はどうですか」 puts forward a noun (a thing, a time, a plan) for the listener to judge or accept, as in 「明日はどうですか」.

similar.title: 〜ましょうか (offer / help)
similar.explanation: With 「〜ましょうか」 the speaker offers to do something themselves: 「コーヒーを入れましょうか」. 「コーヒーはいかがですか」 lets the listener decide whether they want it. Both are used when looking after guests.

similar.title: 〜こんな・そんな・あんな・どんな
similar.explanation: Both belong to the ど- question words. 「どんな」 + noun asks about kind or nature (「どんな人ですか」 = What kind of person is he?), while 「〜はどうですか」 asks for an evaluation or impression (「その人はどうですか」 = How is that person?).

meaning: Says how many times something is done within a period of time: “... times a day / a week”.
connection: Time-period noun + に + number + 回／度

senses.label: ... times per ...
senses.meaning: Tells how many times something happens in a unit of time. The period goes before 「に」; the number of times goes before 「回」.
senses.connection: 一日・一週間・一か月・一年, etc. + に + number + 回
examples: I take medicine three times a day.
I swim in the pool twice a week.
I watch a movie once a month.

senses.label: Asking how often
senses.meaning: Use 「何回」 to ask how often: “How many times a ...?” Answer with the same pattern.
senses.connection: Time-period noun + に + 何回 + 〜ますか
examples: How many times a week do you play sports?
How many times a day do you brush your teeth?

senses.label: Once in a long while
senses.meaning: 「〜に一度」 also shows frequency. When 「十年に一度」 or 「百年に一度」 describes a noun, it means something very rare.
senses.connection: Time-period noun + に + 一度 (+ の + noun)
examples: I go back to my country once a year.
This is the heaviest snow in ten years.

notes: The number before 「回」 often changes its sound, and misreadings are common: 「一回（いっかい）」「六回（ろっかい）」「八回（はっかい／はちかい）」「十回（じゅっかい）」.
「三回」 means “three times”, but 「三回目」 means “the third time” — a completely different meaning. Be especially careful with medicine packets and instructions.
Before 「に」 you need a word for a span of time: 「週に二回」 means “twice a week”, but 「月曜日に二回」 means “twice on Monday” and does not describe a weekly frequency.
「一度に」 means “at one time, all at once”, not a frequency: 「一度に三錠飲む」 = take three tablets at once. ✕ Don't read it as “take one tablet, three times”.

work.title: Equipment checks
work.description: The person in charge explains how often a machine is inspected.
work.example: We inspect this machine once every six months.

etymology: Here 「に」 marks the unit for a rate, like “per”. 「回」 originally meant “to turn, go around once”, and came to mean “times”. 「度」 originally meant “measure, scale”, and also came to mean “times”.
formation: It is built as time-span noun + 「に」 + number + 「回」 (or 「度」). Here 「に」 marks the basis for distribution, treating a span such as 「一日」 or 「週」 as one unit; 「回」 and 「度」 are counters for occurrences. “Put so many times into one unit” gives the frequency meaning “... times per ...”. Replace the number with 「何」 and you ask how often; when the span is long and the count is one (「十年に一度」), it naturally extends to a sense of rarity: “once in a blue moon”.

similar.title: 〜おきに
similar.explanation: 「〜おきに」 means “every other ...”, focusing on the gap: 「一日おきに」 = every other day. 「一日に一回」 gives the number of times per unit of time. Note that 「二日おきに」 means skipping two days (once every three days), which is not the same as 「二日に一回」.

similar.title: 〜ごとに
similar.explanation: 「〜ごとに」 means “every ... (once)”: 「一時間ごとに」 = once every hour, focusing on the repeated points. 「〜に〜回」 says directly how many times something happens in a period, so it is better for saying “how many times”.

similar.title: 〜につき
similar.explanation: 「〜につき」 also means “per ...”, but it is mostly used in written contexts such as prices and rules: 「一人につき千円」. For how often something happens in a period, 「〜に〜回」 is the normal choice.

similar.title: 〜ずつ
similar.explanation: 「〜ずつ」 shows equal distribution or the same amount each time: 「一日に二錠ずつ飲む」 = take two tablets each day. It often appears together with 「〜に〜回」: 「ずつ」 gives the amount each time, 「〜に〜回」 gives the number of times.

meaning: Says that two things are the same: “the same as ...”.

senses.label: Same as (predicate)
senses.meaning: Comes at the end of the sentence and says A and B are the same. The negative is 「〜と同じではない」 or 「〜と違う」.
senses.connection: AはBと同じだ／同じです
examples: My birthday is the same day as my mother's.
These shoes are the same as my old ones.

senses.label: The same ... as (before a noun)
senses.meaning: Describes the noun after it: “the same ... as ...”. 「同じ」 goes straight before a noun, with no 「な」.
senses.connection: Bと同じ + noun (クラス・会社・色, etc.)
examples: I go to the same school as my older brother.
Do you have a pen in the same color as this one?

senses.label: In the same way as
senses.meaning: 「〜と同じように」 describes a verb: “do it the same way as ...”.
senses.connection: Bと同じように + verb
examples: Please pronounce it the same way the teacher does.

senses.label: A and B are the same
senses.meaning: List the two things with 「と」, then say 「は同じだ」: “A and B are the same.”
senses.connection: AとBは同じだ／AもBも同じだ
examples: My older sister and I are in the same class.
These two kanji have the same meaning.

notes: 「同じ」 takes no 「な」 before a noun: ✕「同じな色」→ ○「同じ色」.
But before 「の」「ので」「のに」 you do add 「な」: ✕「同じのに」→ ○「同じなのに」「同じなので」.
Don't mix up 「同じ」 (the same) and 「一緒」 (together); the meanings are completely different: 「兄と同じ学校に行く」 = go to the same school as my brother; 「兄と一緒に学校に行く」 = go to school together with my brother.

daily.description: You see what your friend ordered and want the same.
daily.example: I'll have the same as him, please.

work.title: Checking a document format
work.description: Confirming that a new document uses the same format as last time.
work.example: The same format as last time is fine.

etymology: 「同じ」 comes from an old adjective 「同じ（おなじ）」. It is a special word that goes straight before a noun without 「な」. The 「と」 marks what is being compared.
formation: It is made of 「と」 and 「同じ」. 「と」 marks what you compare with, like “as” or “with”, and 「同じ」 means “the same”. “The same as A” is 「Aと同じ」: add 「だ」 to make it a predicate, put it straight before a noun to modify it, or add 「ように」 to use it adverbially. 「同じ」 is generally thought to have been an adjective in old Japanese, which is why modern Japanese puts its stem directly before a noun instead of adding 「な」 like ordinary na-adjectives.

similar.title: 〜ような・〜ように・〜みたいな (simile / example)
similar.explanation: 「〜のような」 and 「〜みたいな」 mean “like ...”: a comparison or an example, where the two things are not actually the same: 「雪のように白い」. 「〜と同じ」 means they really are the same: 「雪と同じ色」.

similar.title: 〜くらい・〜ぐらい (degree)
similar.explanation: 「AくらいB」 says the degree is about the same as A: 「父くらい背が高い」. To say “equally”, it is often combined with 「同じ」 as 「父と同じくらい背が高い」, which stresses equality more than 「くらい」 alone.

similar.title: 〜も同然だ
similar.explanation: 「〜も同然だ」 also contains 「同」 and means “as good as ..., no different from ...”: 「勝ったも同然だ」. It is an exaggerated, figurative judgment, while 「〜と同じ」 states actual sameness, usually about concrete things.

similar.title: 〜と同時に
similar.explanation: 「〜と同時に」 is also built from 「と」 + 「同（じ）」, but 「同時」 means “the same moment”, so the pattern means “at the same time as ...”: 「ベルが鳴ると同時に走り出した」. 「〜と同じ」 is about having the same content or nature.

meaning: Pronouns that point to things: “this”, “that”, “that (over there)” and “which”, chosen by distance from the speaker and the listener.
connection: Used alone, as subject, object, etc. (これは／それを／どれが, etc.)

senses.label: これ: this
senses.meaning: Points to a thing near the speaker: “this (one)”. It can stand alone as subject or object.
senses.connection: これ + は／が／を, etc.
examples: This is my book.
I'll take this one, please.

senses.label: それ: that (near you)
senses.meaning: Points to a thing near the listener. It also refers to what the other person just said: “that”.
senses.connection: それ + は／が／を, etc.
examples: What is that?
A: Tomorrow is a day off. B: That's nice.

senses.label: あれ: that (over there)
senses.meaning: Points to a thing far from both speaker and listener. It also refers to a past event both people remember: “that”.
senses.connection: あれ + は／が／を, etc.
examples: That's the station over there.
That was a fun trip, wasn't it?

senses.label: どれ: which
senses.meaning: A question word: “which one?” among three or more things. As a subject, use 「が」, not 「は」.
senses.connection: どれ + が／を／です, etc.
examples: Which one is your umbrella?
Which one will you have?

notes: Don't use 「これ・それ・あれ」 to refer to people — it is very rude. Use 「こちら」 when introducing someone: ✕「これは田中さんです」→ ○「こちらは田中さんです」.
These words are pronouns and cannot go directly before a noun: ✕「これ本」→ ○「この本」.
When 「どれ」 is the subject, use 「が」, not 「は」: ✕「どれは安いですか」→ ○「どれが安いですか」. To choose between two things, use 「どちら」.
For something just mentioned that the listener doesn't know about, use 「それ」. 「あれ」 is understood as “that thing we both know about”, which will leave the listener confused.

etymology: Japanese demonstratives come in sets called “ko-so-a-do”: 「こ」 is near the speaker, 「そ」 near the listener, 「あ」 far from both, and 「ど」 is the question form. 「〜れ」 is the ending for things. The same system includes 「ここ」 (places) and 「この」 (before nouns).
formation: Each word is a distance prefix plus the ending 「れ」, meaning “thing”. 「こ」 is near the speaker, 「そ」 near the listener, 「あ」 far from both, and 「ど」 asks a question. The prefix tells you “where”, the ending tells you “what kind”: 「〜れ」 is a thing, 「〜こ」 a place, 「〜の」 goes before a noun, and 「〜んな」 is a kind. Because 「〜れ」 makes them noun-like pronouns, they can take 「は・が・を」 directly, but they cannot modify a noun directly.

similar.title: 〜この・その・あの・どの + noun
similar.explanation: Both belong to the こそあど family. 「この・その・あの・どの」 must be followed by a noun (「この本」); 「これ・それ・あれ・どれ」 stand on their own (「これは本です」).

similar.title: 〜ここ・そこ・あそこ・どこ
similar.explanation: Same こそあど family, different endings: 「〜れ」 refers to things, 「〜こ」 to places. 「これは何ですか」 asks about an object; 「ここはどこですか」 asks about a location.

similar.title: 〜こんな・そんな・あんな・どんな
similar.explanation: Same こそあど family. 「こんな・そんな」 mean “this kind of, that kind of”, focus on nature or type, and are followed by a noun. 「これ」 points directly to one specific thing.

meaning: Words placed before a noun to show which one is meant: “this ...”, “that ...”, “that ... (over there)”, “which ...”.
connection: この／その／あの／どの + noun

senses.label: この: this ...
senses.meaning: Describes something near the speaker: “this ...”. It must be followed by a noun.
senses.connection: この + noun
examples: This book is interesting.
How much is this bag?

senses.label: その: that ... (near you)
senses.meaning: Describes something near the listener, or something just mentioned: “that ...”.
senses.connection: その + noun
examples: Is that umbrella yours?
I met a friend yesterday. That person is a doctor.

senses.label: あの: that ... (over there)
senses.meaning: Describes something far from both people, or a person or thing both people know: “that ...”.
senses.connection: あの + noun
examples: Who is that person over there?
The ramen at that shop was good, wasn't it?

senses.label: どの: which ...
senses.meaning: A question word: “which ...?” among three or more. It is followed by a noun.
senses.connection: どの + noun + が／を, etc.
examples: Which train will you take?
Which color do you like?

notes: They can't stand alone; they must be followed by a noun: ✕「このはペンです」→ ○「これはペンです」 or 「このペンは…」.
Calling the listener, your boss or a guest 「この人」 or 「あの人」 in their presence sounds rude and distant. Say 「こちらの方」「あちらの方」 instead.
「どの」 is for choosing among three or more; for two, use 「どちらの」: ✕「赤と青、どの色がいい？」→ ○「どちらの色がいい？」.
For a person or thing just mentioned that the listener doesn't know, use 「その」. 「あの」 implies you both know it; using it wrongly makes the listener think they are supposed to know.

etymology: Made from a ko-so-a-do prefix plus 「の」, which links to a noun: 「こ＋の」, 「そ＋の」, 「あ＋の」, 「ど＋の」. That's why they only come before a noun and describe it.
formation: Each word is a こそあど prefix plus the linking particle 「の」: 「こ＋の」「そ＋の」「あ＋の」「ど＋の」. 「の」 works like “of” or the possessive 's, so 「この」 originally meant “of this side”, and the whole word modifies a noun. Because it ends in 「の」, it behaves like noun + 「の」: it can only come before a noun and can't be a subject or object on its own.

similar.title: 〜これ・それ・あれ・どれ
similar.explanation: Same こそあど family. The 「これ」 series are pronouns and stand alone; the 「この」 series must be followed by a noun. 「これは本です」 and 「この本は…」 have different structures.

similar.title: 〜こんな・そんな・あんな・どんな
similar.explanation: Same こそあど family. 「この本」 refers to one particular book; 「こんな本」 means “this kind of book”, focusing on nature or type.

similar.title: 〜ここ・そこ・あそこ・どこ
similar.explanation: Same こそあど family. The 「ここ」 series stands alone to show a place; for “the ... of this place”, say 「ここの」 + noun (「ここのラーメン」), not 「この」.

meaning: Words that point to places: “here”, “there”, “over there” and “where”.
connection: Used alone, as subject or predicate, or with particles (ここは／そこに／どこへ, etc.)

senses.label: ここ: here
senses.meaning: Points to where the speaker is, or nearby: “here”.
senses.connection: ここ + は／に／で／から, etc.
examples: This is the library.
Please write your name here.

senses.label: そこ: there (near you)
senses.meaning: Points to where the listener is, or nearby. It also refers to a place just mentioned: “there”.
senses.connection: そこ + は／に／で, etc.
examples: The restroom is right there.
There's a bookstore in front of the station. I'll wait for you there.

senses.label: あそこ: over there
senses.meaning: Points to a place far from both speaker and listener: “over there”.
senses.connection: あそこ + は／に／で, etc.
examples: There's a bank over there.
That restaurant over there is cheap.

senses.label: どこ: where
senses.meaning: A question word asking about a place: “where?” Add 「か」 for “somewhere”; use 「も〜ない」 for “nowhere”.
senses.connection: どこ + ですか／に／へ／で, etc.
examples: Where is the station?
Where are you going for summer vacation?

notes: Asking guests or clients about a place or their company with 「どこ」 sounds casual; use 「どちら」: ✕「会社はどこですか」→ ○「どちらの会社ですか」「お国はどちらですか」.
To say “there is ... here”, use 「に」, not 「で」: ✕「ここで銀行があります」→ ○「ここに銀行があります」. 「で」 is for doing an action there.
The far form is 「あそこ」, not 「あこ」. 「あそこ」 is also used for a place neither of you can see but both know.

daily.title: Asking the way
daily.description: A tourist asks a passerby where the station is.
daily.example: Excuse me, where is the station?

daily.title: Meeting a friend
daily.description: On the phone, telling a friend where you are.
daily.example: I'm in front of the bookstore now. Come over here.

daily.title: Giving directions
daily.description: Pointing far away to show where the convenience store is.
daily.example: The convenience store is over there.

work.title: Showing a new coworker around
work.description: Pointing to the copier across the office.
work.example: The copy machine is over there.

work.title: Showing someone their desk
work.description: Telling a new coworker where they sit.
work.example: Your desk is right there, Tanaka-san.

etymology: Part of the ko-so-a-do system. 「〜こ」 is the ending for places: 「こ＋こ」, 「そ＋こ」, 「ど＋こ」. The far form is not 「あこ」 but 「あそこ」. It is thought to come from older words like 「かしこ」, so it is an exception.
formation: Each word is a こそあど prefix plus 「こ」, an element meaning “place”: 「こ＋こ」「そ＋こ」「ど＋こ」 — near me, near you, where. The far form is not 「あこ」 but 「あそこ」, an exception generally thought to come from an older form. Since they are place nouns themselves, they take case particles such as 「に・で・へ・から」 directly, giving “here”, “from there” and so on.

similar.title: 〜これ・それ・あれ・どれ
similar.explanation: Same こそあど family. The 「これ」 series refers to things, the 「ここ」 series to places: 「これは何ですか」 asks about an object, 「ここはどこですか」 asks about a location.

similar.title: 〜この・その・あの・どの + noun
similar.explanation: Same こそあど family. The 「この」 series must be followed by a noun; the 「ここ」 series stands alone for a place, and to modify a noun you say 「ここの店」.

similar.title: 〜question word + か (indefinite)
similar.explanation: 「どこか」, from 「どこ」 + 「か」, means “somewhere”, not “where?”: 「どこか行きますか」 = Are you going somewhere? (answered yes or no); 「どこへ行きますか」 = Where are you going? (answered with a place).

meaning: After a noun, marks the starting point in time or place, or the source of an action or information, or the place passed through (“from …”); after a clause, gives a reason that the speaker subjectively puts forward (“because …”).
connection: Noun + から (starting point, source, route); verb / adjective (plain or polite) + から; noun / na-adjective + だから (reason)

senses.label: Starting time
senses.meaning: Shows when an action or state begins: “from ... (o'clock)”. Often paired with 「まで」.
senses.connection: Time noun + から (〜まで)
examples: Class starts at nine.
I work from Monday to Friday.

senses.label: Starting place
senses.meaning: Shows where movement starts: “from (a place)”.
senses.connection: Place noun + から + 来る・出る・帰る, etc.
examples: I came from China.
I walk from the station to my house.

senses.label: Source (person or thing)
senses.meaning: Shows where something or some information comes from: “from (someone)”. Often used with 「もらう」, 「借りる」 and 「聞く」.
senses.connection: Person + から + もらう・借りる・聞く・届く, etc.
examples: I got a letter from my mother.
I heard about that from my teacher.

senses.label: Way in or out
senses.meaning: Shows the opening you pass through: “through (a window, door)”.
senses.connection: 窓・門・入口, etc. + から + 入る・出る
examples: A cat came in through the window.
Please come in through this entrance.

senses.label: Giving a reason
senses.meaning: Explains the basis for your judgment, decision, or request. The main clause can be a command, request, or intention. In this respect it is freer than 「ので」.
senses.connection: Verb / i-adjective (plain) + から; noun / na-adjective + だから
examples: We're out of time, so please hurry.
I'm tired today, so I'm going to bed early.
It's raining, so I don't want to go out.

senses.label: Reason at the end
senses.meaning: 「〜からだ／〜からです」 at the end of a sentence explains the reason afterward, often in the pattern 「〜のは〜からだ」. When answering 「どうして」, you can give just the reason.
senses.connection: Plain form + からだ／からです
examples: The reason I was late is that the train stopped.
“Why were you off?” “Because I had a fever.”

senses.label: Polite form + から
senses.meaning: Using polite 「〜ますから」 or 「〜ですから」 before it sounds more courteous. Common when explaining things to guests or elders.
senses.connection: Verb masu-form / です + から
examples: Tomorrow is a day off, so please take it easy.
I'll be right back, so please wait here.

notes: Verb te-form + 「から」 means “after ...”, but plain form + 「から」 means “because” — completely different: 「食べてから行く」 = go after eating; 「食べるから行く」 = go because I'm going to eat.
With some verbs, the place you leave can only take 「を」: ✕「大学から卒業する」→ ○「大学を卒業する」.
For a range, pair 「から」 with 「まで」: ✕「九時から五時に働く」→ ○「九時から五時まで働く」.

「から」 carries the speaker's own assertion. Using it to explain lateness or time off to a superior or client sounds like you're insisting you're right or making excuses; use 「ので」 instead: ✕「電車が遅れたから、遅刻しました」 → ○「電車が遅れたので、遅刻してしまいました」.
After nouns and na-adjectives add 「だ」: ○「雨だから」, not ✕「雨から」. With 「ので」 it's 「雨なので」; don't mix the two up.

daily.example: It's raining today, so let's watch a movie at home.

daily.title: Warning a child
daily.description: Followed by a command, 「から」 sounds natural.
daily.example: It's dangerous, so don't touch it!

work.example: The meeting will start at 2 p.m.

work.example: There's a test tomorrow, so get to bed early, okay?

etymology: 「から」 was originally a case particle for a starting point or a route (“from …”). It is generally thought to be related to the old word 「柄（から）」, meaning “by way of, nature, cause.” In Old Japanese it mainly marked the place passed through, then extended to the starting point, and from there to the conjunctive particle for reasons, which became common from the medieval period on.
formation: The core meaning is “starting from ….” After a noun, the starting point can be a time (「九時から」), a place (「駅から」) or a source (「母から」); entering through an opening such as a window gives the place passed through (「窓から」). After a clause, treating one event as the starting point of another gives a reason: 「時間がないから急ぐ」 = starting from “there is no time,” I conclude “I'll hurry.” Since the speaker sets this starting point, it sounds subjective and can be followed directly by commands, requests or resolutions; this is also why it is less polite than 「ので」, which states the reason as an objective fact.

similar.title: 〜より (starting point / written)
similar.explanation: 「より」 also marks a starting point, but only in written language such as notices and letters: 「会議は十時より行います」. In everyday conversation, always use 「から」.

similar.title: 〜から〜まで
similar.explanation: 「から」 combined with 「まで」 marks the start and end of a range: 「九時から五時まで」「東京から大阪まで」.

similar.title: 〜ので
similar.explanation: Both express reasons. 「から」 is subjective and can be followed directly by commands or intentions; 「ので」 is objective and gentle, and is preferred for giving reasons in polite situations.

similar.title: 〜のだから・〜んだから
similar.explanation: An emphatic form of the same origin: it presents the reason as a fact both sides already know, "since..., you should...", often with a tone of blame or persuasion (「子どもじゃないんだから、自分でやりなさい」).

similar.title: 〜からこそ
similar.explanation: Same origin: adding 「こそ」 stresses "precisely because...", highlighting that this is the real reason (「好きだからこそ厳しく言う」).

meaning: Denies the first item and affirms the second: “not A but B”, used to correct a misunderstanding or state the real situation; 「じゃなくて」 is colloquial, 「ではなくて」 and 「ではなく」 are written.
connection: Noun / stem of a な-adjective + じゃなくて / ではなくて / ではなく / でなく + noun (だ); plain-form verb / い-adjective + の (ん) + ではなく / じゃなくて

senses.label: Not A but B (casual)
senses.meaning: First deny A, then give the correct B. Used to correct a misunderstanding or your own words. 「じゃなくて」 is casual.
senses.connection: Noun A + じゃなくて + noun B
examples: This isn't tea, it's coffee.
I'm not a student, I'm a teacher.
It's not today, it's tomorrow.

senses.label: Not A but B (formal)
senses.meaning: 「ではなくて」 and 「ではなく」 are more formal. They are common in writing, the news and formal situations.
senses.connection: Noun A + ではなくて／ではなく + noun B
examples: The meeting is on the fifth floor, not the third.
What matters is not money but health.

senses.label: Correcting an action
senses.meaning: After a verb or a sentence, use 「〜のではなく／〜んじゃなくて」: “not ..., but ...”.
senses.connection: Verb plain form + の (ん) + ではなく／じゃなくて
examples: Don't just memorize it. Understand it.
I'm not angry, I'm worried about you.

senses.label: Written contracted form (でなく)
senses.meaning: Verbs and adjectives use 「のではなく」. In writing you can drop 「は」 and say 「でなく」.
senses.connection: Plain form + のではなく; noun + でなく
examples: Instead of running away, you should face the problem.
What matters is not the result but the process.

notes: The point is the second part, B: 「コーヒーじゃなくて、お茶」 = what I want is tea. Swap A and B and you say the exact opposite.
「だけじゃなくて」 means “not only ... but also ...”. Leave out 「だけ」 and it becomes “not ... but ...”: 「英語だけじゃなくて中国語も話せる」 ≠ 「英語じゃなくて中国語を話せる」.
After verbs and i-adjectives, add 「の／ん」: ✕「覚えるじゃなくて」→ ○「覚えるんじゃなくて」; ✕「高いじゃなくて」→ ○「高いんじゃなくて」.
Correcting a boss or client with a blunt 「〜じゃなくて」 sounds harsh, as if you were talking back. Say 「恐れ入りますが、〜ではなく〜です」 instead.
「ではなくても」 and 「でなくてもいい」 mean “even if it isn't ...”, which is not this grammar point.

daily.example: Excuse me, I ordered it hot, not iced.

daily.example: I'm not Japanese, I'm Chinese.

etymology: Made of the continuative 「で」 of the copula 「だ」, the topic/contrast particle 「は」 and the continuative 「なく」 of 「ない」 (+ 「て」), i.e. the pause form of 「ではない」. 「では」 contracts to 「じゃ」 in speech; in writing 「て」 is often dropped to give 「ではなく」, and in a still more formal style 「は」 is dropped too, giving 「でなく」.
formation: Built from 「で」 (continuative of the copula 「だ」) + 「は」 (topic/contrast) + 「なく」 (continuative of 「ない」) + 「て」 (connective). 「Aではない」 means “it is not A”; replacing the final 「ない」 with the continuative 「なく（て）」 means the sentence does not end there but goes on, giving the structure “deny A first, then give B”. 「は」 carries contrast and hints “A is not it; something else is”, so the correct B naturally follows — this is where the “correction” meaning comes from. 「じゃ」 is the spoken contraction of 「では」; 「ではなく」 drops 「て」 and 「でなく」 drops 「は」 as well, becoming more formal each time, which explains the spoken/written split between the senses. With verbs and い-adjectives, 「の（ん）」 first turns them into a noun-like unit, which then fits the same “not A but B” frame (「覚えるのではなく、理解する」).

similar.title: 〜じゃない・〜ではありません
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「じゃない」 is the spoken form of 「ではない」. 「〜じゃない」 only says “it's not A” and ends the sentence; 「〜じゃなくて」 denies A and then goes on to give the correct B.

similar.title: 〜だけでなく
similar.explanation: 「AだけでなくB」 means “not only A but also B” — both A and B are true. With 「AじゃなくてB」 only B is true. One 「だけ」 makes all the difference.

similar.title: 〜というより
similar.explanation: 「AというよりB」 means “B rather than A”: it doesn't fully deny A, it just says B fits better. 「AじゃなくてB」 clearly denies A.

similar.title: 〜代わりに
similar.explanation: 「代わりに」 means using B “in place of” A, and A is not necessarily wrong (「肉の代わりに豆腐を使う」). 「ではなく」 corrects, so A itself is denied.

meaning: Expresses the speaker's thoughts, opinions or guesses: “I think ...”.
connection: Plain form + と思う (noun / na-adjective + だと思う)

senses.label: Giving an opinion
senses.meaning: States your view or judgment: “I think ...”. 「〜と思います」 sounds softer than a flat statement.
senses.connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form + と思う; noun / na-adjective + だと思う
examples: I think this movie is interesting.
I think Japanese is difficult.
I think he's a good person.

senses.label: Guessing
senses.meaning: Makes a guess about something uncertain: “I think ... will ...”. Often used with 「たぶん」 or 「きっと」.
senses.connection: Plain form + と思う (たぶん・きっと〜と思う)
examples: I think it will rain tomorrow.
I think Tanaka-san probably won't come.

senses.label: Negating or asking opinions
senses.meaning: To deny a view, use 「〜とは思わない」. To ask someone's opinion, use 「〜と思いますか」.
senses.connection: Plain form + とは思わない／と思いますか
examples: I don't believe that story is true.
Do you think these clothes are expensive?

notes: 「〜と思う」 only expresses the speaker's own thoughts: 「田中さんは行くと思う」 means “I think Tanaka will go”, not “Tanaka thinks”. For a third person's thoughts, use 「田中さんは行きたいと思っている」.
Nouns and na-adjectives need 「だ」: ✕「きれいと思う」→ ○「きれいだと思う」.
With the volitional form it means “intend”; with the plain form it is a guess: 「行こうと思う」 = I'm thinking of going; 「行くと思う」 = I think (someone) will go.
When reporting a confirmed fact to your boss, don't add 「と思います」 — it sounds unsure, as if you were dodging responsibility: ✕「会議は三時からだと思います」 (when already confirmed) → ○「会議は三時からです」.
The negative usually goes in the first part: 「来ないと思う」 is more natural than 「来るとは思わない」.

daily.description: After eating with a friend, you share your impression.
daily.example: I think this place is really good.

daily.description: Before going out, you guess the weather to your family.
daily.example: I think it'll rain from the afternoon.

daily.description: Trying on clothes and asking a friend what they think.
daily.example: Do you think this color suits me?

work.description: Gently giving your opinion in a meeting.
work.example: I think this plan needs a little more time.

work.title: Estimating progress
work.description: Your boss asks if the work will be done on time.
work.example: I think it will be done by Friday.

etymology: 「思う」 originally meant “to think in one's heart, to long for”. 「と」 is the quoting particle. It puts the thought in front like a quoted sentence.
formation: It is built as quoted content + 「と」 + 「思う」. 「と」 is the quotation particle that wraps the preceding words as content, and 「思う」 means “to think, in your mind”. In other words, you quote your own judgment as words said inside your head, so the sentence naturally sounds subjective and soft — “this is just my view” — which suits opinions and guesses. Because a complete sentence is being quoted, nouns and na-adjectives need 「だ」 to finish it; and an intention is quoted with the volitional form, as the inner words 「行こう」.

similar.title: 〜と思っている
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「〜と思っている」 shows a thought held over time and can be used for third persons: 「彼は日本へ行きたいと思っている」. 「〜と思う」 is mostly the speaker's judgment in the moment.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うと思う
similar.explanation: Same origin. After the volitional form (「行こう」「食べよう」) it shows your own intention: 「明日行こうと思う」. Plain form + 「と思う」 gives an opinion or a guess.

similar.title: 〜でしょう (guess / confirmation)
similar.explanation: 「でしょう」 also expresses a guess, but it sounds more objective and is common in weather forecasts. 「と思う」 colors the statement as the speaker's personal view.

similar.title: 〜だろうと思う
similar.explanation: Same origin. Adding 「だろう」 before 「と思う」 makes the guess less certain and softer: 「明日は雨だろうと思う」.

meaning: Reports what someone said, or gives a name: “say ...”, “be called ...”.

senses.label: Direct quotation
senses.meaning: Puts someone's exact words in 「」 and reports them as they were: “(someone) said, '...'”.
senses.connection: 「Exact words」 + と言う／と言いました
examples: My mother said, “Go to bed early.”
In Japan, people say “itadakimasu” before eating.

senses.label: Indirect quotation
senses.meaning: Reports the content in the plain form, not the exact words: “(someone) said that ...”.
senses.connection: Plain form + と言う／と言いました (noun / na-adjective + だと言う)
examples: Tanaka-san said he won't come tomorrow.
My friend said this shop is cheap.

senses.label: Names and words
senses.meaning: Gives a name or says what a word is: “be called ...”. To ask what something is called, use 「何と言いますか」.
senses.connection: Name / word + と言います／何と言いますか
examples: My name is Wang.
What is this called in Japanese?
This flower is called sakura.

notes: Don't use 「言う」 to ask the listener's or a client's name: ✕「お名前は何と言いますか」→ ○「お名前は何とおっしゃいますか」. The formal way to give your own name is 「〜と申します」.
In indirect quotes, change the person, or the meaning changes completely: if Tanaka says 「私が行く」, report it as 「田中さんは自分が行くと言った」. 「田中さんは私が行くと言った」 would mean Tanaka said that I (the speaker) would go.
「言う」 is pronounced 「ゆう」, but it must be written 「いう」: ✕「何とゆう」→ ○「何という」.
To pass on what someone said, 「〜と言っていました」 usually sounds more natural than 「〜と言いました」.

work.title: Answering the phone

work.example: Excuse me, may I have your name?

etymology: 「言う」 originally meant “to put into words”. 「と」 is the quoting particle that marks what was said. 「言う」 is pronounced 「ゆう」 but written 「いう」.
formation: It is built as quoted content + 「と」 + 「言う」. 「と」 is the quotation particle that wraps the preceding words as “what was said”: carry over the exact words in 「」 and you have a direct quote; change them to plain form and blend them into the sentence and you have an indirect quote. 「AはBと言う」 literally means “A is said (by people) to be B”, which extends to naming: “A is called B” (「この花は桜と言います」).

similar.title: 〜という (called)
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「AというB」 is followed by a noun and means “a B called A” (「田中という人」); it is usually written in kana. 「〜と言う」 is a predicate meaning “say ...”.

similar.title: 〜と言っていた (reporting)
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「〜と言っていた」 is used specifically to pass on what a third person said: 「先生が明日休みだと言っていた」. It sounds more natural than 「〜と言った」.

similar.title: 〜って (quote / topic)
similar.explanation: 「って」 is the colloquial form of 「と（言う）」: 「明日休みだって」 (I heard tomorrow's a day off). In formal situations, use 「と言う」.

similar.title: 〜と思う (I think)
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use 「と」 to quote content. 「と言う」 quotes words spoken aloud; 「と思う」 quotes thoughts in your head.

meaning: Uses B as a standard and says A is more so in some way: “A is more ... than B”.
connection: Noun A + は + noun B + より + adjective / verb

senses.label: A is more ... than B
senses.meaning: What comes before 「より」 is the standard, B. The sentence describes the topic, A: “A is ...-er than B”.
senses.connection: AはBより + i-adjective／na-adjective／verb
examples: Tokyo is bigger than Osaka.
Today is colder than yesterday.
My older brother is taller than me.

senses.label: Stronger emphasis
senses.meaning: 「よりも」 is stronger than 「より」 and stresses what you compare with.
senses.connection: AはBよりも + adjective / verb
examples: Health is more important than money.
My younger sister is even better at cooking than I am.

senses.label: Comparing actions
senses.meaning: With verbs, it compares two ways of doing things or their degree: “more ... than ...”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + より + 〜ほうがいい, etc. / noun + より + verb
examples: The train gets there earlier than the bus.
Rather than watching, I want to try it myself.

notes: 「より」 attaches to the standard of comparison; put it in the wrong place and the meaning flips: 「東京は大阪より大きい」 = Tokyo is bigger than Osaka. If you mean the same thing, ✕「大阪は東京より大きい」 says the opposite.
The adjective itself does the comparing, so you don't need a word for “more” or an “-er” ending: ○「今日は昨日より寒い」. To stress a big gap, use 「ずっと」: 「ずっと寒い」.
When answering 「AとBとどちらが〜」, use 「〜のほうが」: ✕「Aが大きいです」→ ○「Aのほうが大きいです」.
Comparing yourself favorably with your boss or a client to their face (「部長より私のほうが詳しいです」) sounds arrogant and rude; avoid it in Japanese workplaces.

daily.title: Talking about the weather
daily.description: Chatting with your family as you head out in the morning.
daily.example: It's warmer today than yesterday, isn't it?

daily.title: Comparing products
daily.description: Comparing the prices of two items in a shop.
daily.example: This one's cheaper than that one.

daily.title: Talking about family
daily.description: Telling a friend about your younger brother.
daily.example: My younger brother is taller than me.

work.description: Telling your boss about this month's sales.
work.example: Sales this month went up compared with last month.

work.title: Comparing plans
work.description: Comparing two plans in a meeting.
work.example: Plan A costs less than Plan B.

etymology: In old Japanese, 「より」 marked a starting point or route (“from”). It later came to mark a standard of comparison (“compared with”). Today 「から」 mostly handles “from”; 「より」 as “from” survives only in writing (「九時より開始」).
formation: It is built as A + 「は」 + B + 「より」 + predicate. 「は」 puts A forward as the topic; 「より」 originally marks a starting point, “from”, and here means “measuring with B as the starting point” — that is, the standard of comparison. “Measured from B, A is big” means “A is bigger than B”. Since 「より」 already marks the standard, the adjective alone can express the comparison with no word for “more”. Adding 「も」 to make 「よりも」 stresses “even compared with B”.

similar.title: 〜より〜のほうが
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「BよりAのほうが〜」 puts the focus on A and is often used to answer “which is more ...?”. 「AはBより〜」 makes A the topic and describes it.

similar.title: 〜と〜とどちらが
similar.explanation: The question pattern for comparing two things: 「AとBとどちらが〜ですか」. Answer with 「〜のほうが」; for statements, use 「AはBより〜」.

similar.title: 〜ほど〜ない
similar.explanation: 「AはBほど〜ない」 means “A is not as ... as B”, making the comparison with a negative; 「AはBより〜」 is a positive comparison. 「今日は昨日ほど寒くない」 ≈ 「昨日は今日より寒かった」.

similar.title: 〜より (starting point / written)
similar.explanation: Another use of the same 「より」: in written language it marks a starting point (「九時より開始」). The comparison meaning comes from “measuring from B as the starting point”.

meaning: A sentence-final 「な」 with two quite different uses: after a plain-form sentence (「なあ」 when lengthened) it expresses the speaker's exclamation, longing or reminiscence, mostly to oneself; after a dictionary-form verb it is a blunt prohibition, “don't ...”.
connection: Plain form + なあ／な (noun・na-adjective + だなあ); verb dictionary form + な (prohibition)

senses.label: Exclamation
senses.meaning: A natural reaction when you see or feel something: “What a ...!”, “So ...!”
senses.connection: i-adjective + なあ; noun / na-adjective + だなあ
examples: It's so hot today.
What a beautiful view.
This cake is so good.

senses.label: Wishes
senses.meaning: After 「〜たい」, 「〜といい」 or 「ほしい」, it shows a wish: “I wish ...”, “I really want ...”.
senses.connection: 〜たいなあ／〜といいなあ／〜がほしいなあ
examples: I really want to go to the beach this summer.
I wish I had a new computer.

senses.label: Looking back
senses.meaning: Used when remembering the past with feeling. Often follows the past form.
senses.connection: Past form + なあ／な
examples: My school days were so much fun.
That trip was great.

senses.label: Strong prohibition
senses.meaning: Directly forbids someone from doing something. Rough and forceful; mostly used by men toward younger people or in emergencies.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + な (行くな, 触るな, するな, 来るな)
examples: Don't touch it, it's dangerous!
No smoking here.
Don't ever come back!

senses.label: Encouragement and comfort
senses.meaning: In phrases like 「心配するな」, 「負けるな」, 「泣くな」, it encourages or comforts. The tone is warm but firm.
senses.connection: 心配するな, 負けるな, 泣くな, 気にするな, 諦めるな
examples: Don't worry. It'll work out.
Don't give up! Keep going to the end!

senses.label: Signs and quoting
senses.meaning: Used on signs and warnings (not aimed at anyone in particular), or as 「〜なと言われた」 to report someone's prohibition.
senses.connection: Dictionary form + な (signs); dictionary form + なと言う／なと言われた
examples: Keep off the grass.
My doctor told me not to drink alcohol.

notes: 「なあ」 and 「な」 are exclamations you make to yourself; saying them directly to a boss or guest sounds casual and rude: ✕「部長、これおいしいなあ」→ ○「おいしいですね」.
Verb dictionary form + 「な」 is a prohibition (「行くな」 = Don't go!) and sounds very rough. For exclamations, verbs usually take 「〜たい」, the た-form or the ない-form: 「行きたいなあ」.
Nouns and na-adjectives need 「だ」: ✕「きれいなあ」→ ○「きれいだなあ」.
It is harsh and very rude toward superiors, elders, guests or strangers. The polite version is 「〜ないでください」, and 「〜ないで」 with people you know: ✕ (to a guest)「触るな」→ ○「触らないでください」.

A sentence-final 「な」 can also be an exclamation: 「よく食べるな」 means "wow, you sure eat a lot", not "don't eat". The prohibitive 「な」 is short and sharp; the exclamatory 「な」 can also follow adjectives and 「だ」, and is often stretched into 「なあ」.

daily.title: Seeing a great view
daily.description: Talking to yourself when you see a beautiful view on a trip.
daily.example: Wow, Mt. Fuji is so beautiful.

daily.title: Envying a friend

daily.example: Hawaii? Lucky you!

daily.example: Stay away from the river.

daily.title: Warning signs

daily.example: Danger! Keep out.

etymology: The exclamatory 「な」 is an old sentence-final particle, and 「なあ」 is simply 「な」 lengthened for stronger feeling; it is generally seen as the same line as the classical particles 「な」 and 「かな」. The prohibitive 「な」 is also a classical sentence-final particle; classical Japanese often used the form 「な〜そ」 (な行きそ = don't go), which later shrank to the sentence-final 「〜な」.
formation: Both are the sentence-final particle 「な」 added to the end of a sentence, but what precedes it differs. Added to a plain-form statement, 「な」 expresses the speaker's feeling; lengthened to 「なあ」 the feeling shows more. It needs no reply from the listener, so it is mostly used as a monologue; after 「〜たい」 it becomes a wish (“I really want to ...”) and after the past form a reminiscence (“those were the days”). Added directly to a dictionary-form verb, it says “no” to the whole action with no cushioning, so it sounds short and forceful: a prohibition. It has nothing to do with the negative 「ない」, and the verb stays affirmative, which is where learners go wrong. Both uses are speaker-centered and informal, so they are risky toward superiors.

similar.title: 〜ね
similar.explanation: 「ね」 is said to the listener to seek agreement: 「暑いですね」. 「なあ」 is mostly an exclamation to yourself: 「暑いなあ」. When talking to someone, 「ね」 is more natural.

similar.title: 〜かな
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「かな」 combines the question particle 「か」 with the exclamatory 「な」 and expresses wondering or uncertainty: 「明日は晴れるかな」. 「なあ」 itself is an exclamation or a wish.

similar.title: 〜ないでください
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both mean "don't ...". 「〜ないでください」 is a polite request you can use with anyone; 「〜な」 is a rude, direct prohibition.

similar.title: 〜てはいけない
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both express prohibition. 「〜てはいけない」 states a rule ("you must not ...") and is more objective; 「〜な」 is the speaker directly forbidding something, and is stronger.

similar.title: 〜てくれと言う・〜なと言う (reported commands)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜なと言う」 simply puts the prohibitive 「な」 inside a quotation: 「医者に飲むなと言われた」 (the doctor told me not to drink). A more polite way to report it is 「飲まないように言われた」.

meaning: Put a plain-form clause directly before a noun to describe it, like “the ... that ...”: verbs (dictionary, た, ない, ている forms), adjectives and noun phrases all work, with no 「の」 in between.
connection: Plain-form clause (verb, adjective, noun + だった, etc.) + noun

senses.label: Dictionary form + noun
senses.meaning: Shows a habit, something planned, or a general fact: “the ... (I) do / will do”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + noun
examples: The coffee I drink every morning is good.
Please tell me the place we're going tomorrow.

senses.label: た-form + noun
senses.meaning: Shows a finished action: “the ... (I) did”.
senses.connection: Verb た-form + noun
examples: This is the book I bought yesterday.
The movie I saw last week was interesting.

senses.label: ない-form + noun
senses.meaning: Shows a negative: “the ... (I) don't / didn't do”.
senses.connection: Verb ない-form + noun
examples: I look up words I don't know in a dictionary.
Some people don't eat meat.

senses.label: ている-form + noun
senses.meaning: Shows an action in progress or an ongoing state. Often used to describe what people are wearing or doing.
senses.connection: Verb ている-form + noun
examples: Who is the person wearing glasses?
The person reading a book over there is my older brother.

senses.label: With a subject
senses.meaning: The subject inside the clause takes 「が」 (or 「の」), not 「は」.
senses.connection: Noun + が + verb plain form + noun
examples: The food my mother makes is delicious.
The town I live in is quiet.
The food my mother makes is the best.

senses.label: Adjective and noun clauses
senses.meaning: い-adjectives go directly before the noun; な-adjectives take 「な」. Noun predicates use 「の」 in the present and 「だった」 in the past.
senses.connection: い-adjective + noun／な-adjective な + noun／noun の・noun だった + noun
examples: A girl with big eyes is laughing.
I listened to a song I loved as a child.
I want to live in a town with good transportation.

notes: Learners often add an extra 「の」: ✕「昨日買ったの本」→ ○「昨日買った本」. The verb goes directly before the noun, with nothing in between.
The subject inside the modifying part takes 「が」 or 「の」, not 「は」: ✕「私は買った本」→ ○「私が買った本」.

Mixing up the dictionary form and the ta-form changes the meaning completely: 「日本へ行く人」 is “a person who is going to Japan”, 「日本へ行った人」 is “a person who has been to Japan”; 「結婚する人」 is “a person who is getting married”, 「結婚した人」 is “a married person”.
For a current state, use 「ている」 or the た-form: 「眼鏡をかけている人」 = a person wearing glasses; 「眼鏡をかける人」 means “a person who (usually, or will) put on glasses” — a different meaning.
Before a noun, na-adjectives take 「な」 and nouns take 「の」 — never 「だ」: ✕「静かだ町」→ ○「静かな町」; ✕「父が医者だ友だち」→ ○「父が医者の友だち」.

daily.description: Showing your family who is in a photo.
daily.example: The person smiling in this photo is my friend.

daily.title: Looking for something

daily.example: Where's the bread I bought yesterday?

daily.title: Recommending a book

daily.example: This is a book by my favorite author.

daily.title: Recommending a restaurant
daily.description: Recommending the ramen shop in front of the station to a friend.
daily.example: The ramen at the shop in front of the station is really good.

work.description: Asking a coworker about the documents you'll use.
work.example: Have you prepared the materials we'll use in the meeting?

work.title: Explaining the situation
work.description: Telling your boss about unfinished work.
work.example: There are three tasks that aren't finished yet.

work.title: Introducing a product
work.description: Presenting a popular product to a client.
work.example: This product is popular with young people.

etymology: Japanese predicates (verbs and adjectives) have an “attributive form” (連体形) used to connect to a noun, hence the term 「連体修飾」, “attributive modification”. In modern Japanese the attributive form of verbs and い-adjectives is identical to the dictionary form, so it looks as if the plain form simply sits in front of the noun.
formation: Japanese modifiers always come before the noun they describe, so a whole plain-form clause can be placed in front of a noun as is: 「昨日買った」 + 「本」 → 「昨日買った本」. Nothing like Chinese “的” is needed, so no 「の」 is added. The clause keeps its own tense and polarity, so the verb form alone distinguishes “will do (dictionary form), did (た-form), doesn't do (ない-form), is doing (ている-form)”; these are forms of one and the same structure, which is why they are one grammar point. Adjectives and noun phrases follow the same principle, except that 「だ」 of nouns and な-adjectives changes to the attributive 「な」 (usually 「の」 after a noun), and the past is 「だった」. Because the clause is just part of the noun phrase, it does not use 「です・ます」, and its subject takes 「が」 or 「の」 rather than 「は」, which marks the topic of the whole sentence.

similar.title: 〜な + noun (na-adjective modification)
similar.explanation: Also noun modification: na-adjectives need 「な」 before a noun (「静かな町」), while the plain form of a verb goes straight before the noun with nothing added.

meaning: When counting in Japanese, you add a counter after the number that shows the type of thing, a bit like “two sheets of paper” or “three bottles of water” in English.
connection: Number + counter (〜つ・〜本・〜人・〜枚, etc.)

senses.label: 〜つ: general
senses.meaning: Works for most objects and abstract things. It only goes up to ten (「とお」); from eleven on, use plain numbers.
senses.connection: ひとつ・ふたつ・みっつ…とお／いくつ
examples: Three apples, please.
I have one question.
How many eggs do you need?

senses.label: 〜人: people
senses.meaning: Counts people. 「一人」 is 「ひとり」, 「二人」 is 「ふたり」, and from three on it's 「〜にん」.
senses.connection: 一人（ひとり）・二人（ふたり）・三人（さんにん）…／何人
examples: There are four people in my family.
There are twenty students in the classroom.

senses.label: 〜本: long, thin things
senses.meaning: Counts long, thin things like pens, bottles, umbrellas and trees. Also used for movies and phone calls. The sound changes: いっぽん, にほん, さんぼん.
senses.connection: 一本（いっぽん）・二本（にほん）・三本（さんぼん）…／何本
examples: I bought two pens.
Three bottles of beer, please.

senses.label: 〜枚: thin, flat things
senses.meaning: Counts thin, flat things like paper, plates, shirts, stamps and tickets.
senses.connection: 一枚・二枚・三枚…／何枚
examples: Five stamps, please.
I have two T-shirts.

senses.label: Other common counters
senses.meaning: 「〜冊」 for books, 「〜台」 for machines and cars, 「〜匹」 for small animals, 「〜杯」 for cups and bowls of food or drink, and 「〜個」 for small objects.
senses.connection: Number + 冊・台・匹・杯・個, etc.
examples: I borrowed three books.
We have two cats at home.
I drank a cup of coffee.

notes: The number before a counter often changes its sound, and misreadings are common: 「一本（いっぽん）」「三本（さんぼん）」「六本（ろっぽん）」「三杯（さんばい）」「六匹（ろっぴき）」.
For people, one and two are 「ひとり・ふたり」 and four is 「よにん」: ✕「いちにん」「ににん」「しにん」. 「し（四）」 sounds the same as 「死」 (death), so it is avoided when counting people.

When giving gifts or visiting someone who is ill, avoid the numbers four and nine (they sound like 「死」 “death” and 「苦」 “suffering”); for example, don't give things in sets of four — it is considered bad luck.
「一日」 read 「ついたち」 is “the first (of the month)”, but read 「いちにち」 it is “one day”; 「二十歳」 is read 「はたち」. Misread them and the meaning changes.
The quantity usually goes directly before the verb, with no particle: 「りんごを三つ買う」. ✕「三つりんごを買う」, following English word order, sounds very unnatural.

etymology: 「助数詞」 means “words that help numbers”. Many counters, such as 「本」, 「枚」, 「冊」 and 「台」, came from Chinese and use on-yomi. 「〜つ」 and 「ひとり・ふたり」 are native Japanese ways of counting.
formation: It is built as number + counter. When counting things in Japanese, you usually can't say just the number; you add a counter showing what unit you are counting by. The choice of counter reflects how things are classified by shape and type: 「本」 originally meant “the root or trunk of a tree” and is used for long, thin things; 「枚」 is for thin, flat things; 「冊」 is for bound books. The native Japanese 「〜つ」 only covers one to ten; above ten you switch to Sino-Japanese counters such as 「個」.

similar.title: 〜目 (ordinal)
similar.explanation: Add 「目」 after a counter and it becomes an ordinal: 「三本目」 = the third bottle, 「二人目」 = the second person. 「三本」 is a quantity, 「三本目」 is an order; mixing them up changes the meaning.

similar.title: 〜に〜回 (frequency)
similar.explanation: 「回」 is also a counter, used for counting occurrences; combined with a span of time as in 「週に三回」, it shows frequency. 「三回」 is a number of times; 「一日に三回」 is a frequency.

similar.title: 〜ずつ
similar.explanation: 「ずつ」 follows a quantity and means “... each”: 「一人二つずつ」 = two for each person. It can't be used alone; it needs a quantity made with a counter in front of it.

meaning: Starts a sentence and shows that it goes against or contrasts with the one before: “but”, “however”. Mostly written.

senses.label: Contrast (written)
senses.meaning: Links two sentences when the second goes against what you'd expect: “but, however”. It sounds stiffer than 「でも」 and is common in writing, speeches and the news.
senses.connection: Sentence. + しかし、sentence.
examples: This shop is cheap. However, the food isn't very good.
I studied very hard. However, I failed the exam.

senses.label: Raising a point
senses.meaning: First accept what was said, then give a different view or a problem. Common in essays and meetings.
senses.connection: Sentence. + しかし、problem / different opinion.
examples: The new plan is a good idea. However, it will cost money.

senses.label: Exclamation (spoken)
senses.meaning: At the start of a sentence, it can add feeling, like “Boy, ...” or “Well, ...”. Mostly used by older men.
senses.connection: しかし、+ exclamation
examples: Boy, it sure is hot today.

notes: 「しかし」 is rather formal and stiff; in a chat with friends it sounds old-fashioned or like a speech. In conversation, use 「でも」 or 「けど」.
It can only start a sentence; it can't sit in the middle like 「が」 or 「けど」: ✕「安いしかし、まずい」→ ○「安い。しかし、まずい」.
Starting your reply to a boss's or client's opinion with 「しかし…」 sounds like you're arguing back. Use 「ただ、〜」 or 「恐れ入りますが、〜」 instead.
In speech, the 「しかし」 in 「しかし、暑いね」 is just an exclamation (“Boy, it sure is hot”) and doesn't show contrast; don't assume there is an opposition.

daily.title: Reading the news
daily.description: A news report uses 「しかし」 to link two contrasting facts.
daily.example: The economy is recovering. However, wages haven't risen much.

daily.title: Writing a diary
daily.description: Writing about how the day turned out differently than expected.
daily.example: It was sunny in the morning. However, it started raining in the afternoon.

work.title: Raising an issue in a meeting
work.description: First praising a proposal, then pointing out a problem.
work.example: This plan is interesting. However, I don't think we have enough time.

work.title: Writing a report
work.description: Explaining a result that went against expectations.
work.example: Sales went up. However, profits went down.

etymology: 「しかし」 is a shortening of old 「しかしながら」 (然しながら). 「しか」 (然) means “so, like that”, so it originally meant “even though it is so”. It can be written 「然し」 or 「併し」, but kana is normal today.
formation: It is generally thought to be a shortening of 「しかしながら（然しながら）」. 「しか（然）」 means “so, like that”, pointing back to what was just said; 「ながら」 means “although”. Together they mean “although it is so, ...” — first acknowledging what came before, then presenting the opposite. Because it points back to the whole previous sentence, it can only stand at the start of the next sentence, as an independent conjunction.

similar.title: 〜でも (sentence-initial: but)
similar.explanation: 「でも」 is strongly colloquial and common in everyday conversation; 「しかし」 is formal and stiff, mostly found in writing and formal speech. Both go at the start of a sentence.

similar.title: 〜が (contrast)
similar.explanation: 「が」 sits in the middle of a sentence, joining two parts (「安いが、まずい」); 「しかし」 begins a new sentence as an independent conjunction.

similar.title: 〜けど・〜けれども
similar.explanation: 「けど」 goes inside a sentence and is common in speech; 「しかし」 is an independent conjunction at the start of a sentence and is more formal.

similar.title: 〜ところが (sentence-initial: however / unexpectedly)
similar.explanation: 「ところが」 shows that the result was unexpected (“but, to my surprise, ...”): 「急いで行った。ところが、店は閉まっていた」. 「しかし」 is a general contrast and doesn't necessarily imply surprise.
